doc.title: Kent Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 22, 2006

chapter: The music business and jazz education
title: Making a living in music today: publicity over music
summary: Jordan says jazz is publicity-oriented, people know Wynton Marsalis's name but not his music, and culture and event-going have changed with the internet.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Well what’s it like to try to make a living in music these days?
And has it changed a lot that you would think in the last 15, 20 years?

Oh yes very definitely. I think part of the problem that has happened with music, especially jazz music, and probably all music, is that it’s really publicity oriented now. You know it’s like somebody may know your name or they may know who you are, but they don’t know your music. I’m telling you. I mean I’ve seen it a thousand times. Well obviously take somebody as famous as Wynton is right now, you know in jazz, and I go to my friends, “Oh yea, I know who Wynton Marsalis, I know who Wynton Marsalis is.” And I’ll say, “Okay really?” “Yeah.” At least they may know that he plays the trumpet. I give them credit for that. And I say, “Well do you know any of his compositions? Do you know of a CD that he may have made or any of his music?” And they say, “No I may not know that but I know who he is.” Whereas before, you know, maybe people would say yeah, well I can name his composition, I know this CD or I went to the place or the performance or the club and heard this music. It’s not the same. I think people, now, with soccer moms and I’m a father myself and kids going to college and all these other things that people have to deal with on a day to day basis, it’s very difficult now I think, to deal with cultural issues. Culture now is well you know is there a mother and a father in the home or two women in the home or two men in the home. That’s quote unquote a culture issue now. You know? Or is it that you — what’s another cultural issue, you know I’m trying to think of the things that have sort of been put out there as Americans losing their culture. You know, it’s more a political kind of a culture versus an artistic type of a culture.

Abortion or pro-abortion, all kinds of issues, war and not war. Whereas before maybe you were dealing with those things in very subtle ways but I think parents made sure that their kids went to musical performances, whether that was jazz, classical music or whatever, they went to movies, they weren’t buying DVDs or videos, you know what I mean?
It was more of an event.

Exactly. It was event-driven. Now you know with the advent of the internet — which is good because I love the internet in terms of sort of the like the universality of it, but in a way because of the mass communication of things, because we get our information so spontaneous now and so quickly now, we’ve lost what it really means to go to an event or to go to a happening or to see something new and different, just because there’s so much information out there and people are dealing with life in a very — how can I say it — anticipatory — it’s sort of like it’s on the edge all the time. You know you can’t really get a chance to really relax and enjoy yourself as much as you can. I mean I have this thing that I say like sometimes when I’m telling my musician friends about doing certain things and you know it’s like somebody can work in a corporation and they’re like, “I don’t

want to deal with the office today, I want to go and have a nice meal, find a babysitter for my kids, go to a movie, go listen to some music and just chill.” And then they go to the club and the musicians are like, “Man I don’t want to be here tonight.” So you know that’s why the executives are trying to get away and the musicians are trying to get away at the same time.
